_readme: Per-animal, per-jurisdiction legal status, for the legal hub and its US map.
STATUS VALUES, which are the map colour buckets:
banned      cannot be kept as a pet, no permit route exists
permit      legal, but a permit or licence is required first
conditional legal without a permit only if a stated condition is met
restricted  on a restricted list, permit regime applies but pet keeping is not clearly ruled out
legal       expressly allowed by name in the jurisdiction own rules
unclear     the rule is genuinely ambiguous for this animal. Render grey,
never as legal. Used where a definition arguably reaches an
animal but does not name it, e.g. Texas ends its list with
"or any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision" and
the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal is not itself listed.
(absent)    not researched, OR researched and no rule found. Which one is
decided by coverage.researched, never by the absence itself.
PER-ENTRY FIELDS beyond status:
sourceId      required, keys into `sources`
cite          the section number
quote         the operative wording, verbatim, where short enough
note          anything a reader needs that the quote does not carry
grandfathered { before, detail } if existing owners are exempt. "Banned"
and "banned unless you already had one" are different answers
to the question being asked.
localOverride true where the state says in terms that cities or counties
may prohibit what the state allows. Without this the map
tells someone in a city with its own ordinance the wrong thing.
permitFor     "personal" or "commercial-exhibition-research". New Jersey
issues a hobbyist permit; California only research, exhibition
and pre-1992 animal care. Both read as "permit" and mean
opposite things.
verifiedOn    ISO date the source was actually read. Exotic pet law moves.
Primary sources only: the regulation, the statute, or the enforcing agency
own page. Never a secondary summary.
NYC is separate from NY because its Health Code is stricter than state law
and covers eight million people. The same applies to any city rule worth mapping.

coverage.note: All 51 states and DC have been researched, plus New York City, but not every animal was checked against every one of them: a jurisdiction was read for the animals on the list at the time. 25 of the 51 have now been read for all 35 animals. So an entry means that jurisdiction was read for that animal and this is what it says, including a status of "legal" which means read and nothing found. No entry means it has NOT been read for that animal and the answer is unknown. Never render a missing entry as unrestricted. coverage.perAnimal below records how far each species actually got.

HI.name: Hawaii
HI.scope: HAR chapter 4-71: the prohibited list at § 4-71-6, the conditionally approved list, and the restricted list at § 4-71-6.5. Hawaii runs an inverted rule, so an animal on none of the three is barred by default rather than unregulated.

PA.name: Pennsylvania
PA.scope: 34 Pa.C.S. § 2961, the Game and Wildlife Code definition of exotic wildlife, as the Game Commission applies it.

VA.name: Virginia
VA.scope: 4VAC15-30-40, the Department of Wildlife Resources rule on importing, possessing and selling nonnative exotic animals. Its subsection A table is the operative list; anything absent from it needs no permit under this section.

NC.name: North Carolina
NC.scope: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-417, the only statewide statute regulating exotic animal possession, and § 153A-131, which delegates the rest to counties. There is no statewide exotic pet permit scheme to read.

NH.name: New Hampshire
NH.scope: Fis 800, the Fish and Game Department rules on importation and possession of wildlife, which is the whole framework: non-controlled, prohibited and controlled lists for both importation and possession.

MO.name: Missouri
MO.scope: RSMo § 578.023, the dangerous wild animal registration statute, and 3 CSR 10-9, the Wildlife Code chapter on confined wildlife. Between them these are the two places Missouri restricts keeping an animal.

KS.name: Kansas
KS.scope: K.S.A. 32-1301 and following, the Dangerous Regulated Animals Act, which is the state's only exotic pet statute. Native wildlife possession is handled separately under KAR 115-20 and was not read for this entry.

SC.name: South Carolina
SC.scope: S.C. Code Title 47 Chapter 2, the large wild cat, non-native bear and great ape ban, and Title 50 Chapter 16, the wildlife importation permit chapter. Native game and furbearer harvest rules elsewhere in Title 50 were not read.

MT.name: Montana
MT.scope: MCA Title 87 chapter 5 part 7 and ARM subchapter 12.6.22, the exotic wildlife scheme. Native Montana species such as the prairie dog and tiger salamander are governed by the separate native wildlife rules, which were not read for this entry.

WV.name: West Virginia
WV.scope: W. Va. Code Chapter 19 Article 34, the Dangerous Wild Animals Act. Native wildlife held in captivity is governed separately under Chapter 20 and was not read for this entry.

AK.name: Alaska
AK.scope: 5 AAC 92.029, the live game possession rule, which is Alaska's whole answer for mammals, birds and reptiles. Invertebrates fall outside the definition of game in AS 16.05.940 and were not researched.

SD.name: South Dakota
SD.scope: ARSD chapter 12:68:18, the Animal Industry Board's nondomestic animal control rules, whose permit list covers mammals. Reptiles, amphibians and native wildlife fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules in ARSD title 41, which were not read for this entry.

AL.name: Alabama
AL.scope: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26, the Game and Fish Division rule on possession, sale, importation and release of certain animals. Native Alabama species are separately protected under the same title and were not researched for this entry.

IN.name: Indiana
IN.scope: 312 IAC 9-11, the wild animal possession permit rule. Its own applicability clause limits it to animals referenced in the rule plus state endangered and threatened species, so an animal on none of the three class lists needs no permit.

ND.name: North Dakota
ND.scope: NDCC chapter 36-01, the Board of Animal Health statute, and NDAC title 48.1, its current rules. NDCC title 20.1 chapter 02 was also read: its permit requirement is for transplanting or introducing animals into the state, meaning release, not pet keeping.

WY.name: Wyoming
WY.scope: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 10, live warm-blooded wildlife, and Chapter 69, live cold-blooded wildlife. Together these are the state's importation and possession framework.

MS.name: Mississippi
MS.scope: 40 Miss. Admin. Code Part 2, Rule 8.3, the inherently dangerous wild animal rule, revised April 2025. Native Mississippi wildlife held in captivity is covered by other rules in the same chapter, which were not read for this entry.

LA.name: Louisiana
LA.scope: LAC Title 76 Part V § 115, potentially dangerous wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats and non-human primates, and LAC Title 76 Part XV § 101, the reptile and amphibian rule as amended January 2025.

OK.name: Oklahoma
OK.scope: OAC 800:25-25, the subchapter classifying wildlife as domesticated and exempting it from licensing. Anything outside the exemption needs an import or export permit and a commercial or noncommercial wildlife breeder's licence rather than being banned.

NE.name: Nebraska
NE.scope: 166 NAC 8, Keeping Wildlife in Captivity, which covers wild birds and wild mammals. Reptiles and amphibians are handled by 166 NAC 10 and the fisheries regulations in 164 NAC and were not read for this entry.

ca-671.title: California Code of Regulations Title 14 § 671, via CDFW Restricted Species Laws and Regulations Manual
ca-671.note: § 671(b) defines (D) detrimental and (W) welfare. § 671.1(a) lists permit types; none covers pet keeping. The only possession permit, Animal Care, requires lawful possession in California before January 1992.

ga-391-4-8-05.title: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 391-4-8-.05, Wild Animals, License Required

ga-dnr-exotics.title: Georgia DNR Law Enforcement, Wild Animals/Exotics
ga-dnr-exotics.note: States the enforcement position: 'The exotic species listed below, except where otherwise noted, may not be held as pets in Georgia.'

hi-4-71-6.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules § 4-71-6, List of Prohibited Animals
hi-4-71-6.note: Also carries the default rule: introduction is 'prohibited except for those animals on the lists' incorporated in § 4-71-6.5.

hi-4-71-6-5.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules § 4-71-6.5, List of Restricted Animals, Part A (research and exhibition)
hi-4-71-6-5.note: Part A animals may be brought in by a university or a licensed exhibitor under permit and may not be kept as pets. Part B, published separately as AR-71RB, is the private and commercial use list and was checked as well: it runs to hoofed stock, giraffes, otters, seals, macropods and three named parrots, and contains none of the animals in this dataset.

dc-8-1808.title: D.C. Code § 8-1808(j), Prohibited conduct
dc-8-1808.note: Closed list. Seven permitted categories; everything else is barred as a household pet.

nyc-161-01.title: New York City Health Code Article 161, Animals (NYC Department of Health official PDF)
nyc-161-01.note: § 161.01 is the list of animals that may not be kept in the five boroughs. It binds regardless of what New York State allows, which is why the city and the state answer differently for several species.

nj-7-25-4-4.title: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4 Exempted Species and 7:25-4.5 Additional Species
nj-7-25-4-4.note: 4.4 is a closed exempt list; 4.5 requires a permit for 'any other' exotic species not exempted.

me-unrestricted.title: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Unrestricted Species List
me-unrestricted.note: Species needing no importation, exhibition or possession permit.

wi-169.title: Wisconsin Statutes Chapter 169, Captive Wildlife
wi-169.note: § 169.01(37) defines wild animal; § 169.11(1)(a) designates harmful wild animals as cougars, ursidae, wild and feral swine. § 169.04(4)(b) exempts most non-native species from licensing.

fl-prohibited.title: Florida FWC Prohibited Nonnative Species List (Ch. 68-5, F.A.C.)
fl-prohibited.note: 16 high-risk reptiles added 25 Feb 2021, effective 29 April 2021. Prohibited species may be possessed only by permit for educational exhibition, research or eradication. Tegu and green iguana owners who held one before 29 April 2021 and applied by October 2021 keep a no-cost, non-transferable personal permit for that animal's life.

ny-11-0103.title: N.Y. Environmental Conservation Law § 11-0103(6)(e), definition of wild animal
ny-11-0103.note: A closed definition: 'includes and is limited to' nonhuman primates and prosimians, Felidae and hybrids, Canidae, Ursidae, venomous reptiles plus named large pythons and monitors, and Crocodylia. § 11-0512 then bars possessing a wild animal as a pet, grandfathering animals held when the section took effect if licensed within six months.

ct-26-40a.title: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-40a, Possession of potentially dangerous animal
ct-26-40a.note: Potentially dangerous animals are 'the felidae... the canidae... the ursidae... and the hominidae', or any hybrid. Narrow: no rodents, marsupials, mustelids or insectivores. Civil penalty up to $2,000 per offence and a class A misdemeanour for a wilful violation.

ma-321-9-01.title: 321 CMR 9.01, Exemption List
ma-321-9-01.note: A closed exemption list of wild vertebrates that may be imported, sold or possessed without a permit. Anything not exempt needs one. Criteria include no significant ecological risk if released and care no more demanding than a common domesticated pet.

ma-131-77.title: M.G.L. c. 131 § 77, and 321 CMR 9.02 List of Domestic Animals
ma-131-77.note: Ferrets are handled as domestic animals under 9.02 rather than on the 9.01 exemption list.

co-w11.title: Colorado 2 CCR 406-11, Chapter W-11, Wildlife Parks and Unregulated Wildlife, § 1103(B)
co-w11.note: 'No license is required for the private possession or purchase of animals, which are included on the unregulated wildlife list or the domestic animal list.' Unregulated does not mean unmonitored: importation rules and local ordinances still apply.

az-r12-4-406.title: Ariz. Admin. Code R12-4-406, Restricted Live Wildlife
az-r12-4-406.note: Restricted wildlife requires the applicable federal licences and permits, an appropriate special licence, or a lawful exemption.

or-609-305.title: Or. Rev. Stat. § 609.305, 'Exotic animal' defined, with § 609.341 permit requirement
or-609-305.note: A closed definition: non-indigenous Felidae except the domestic cat, nonhuman primates, non-wolf non-indigenous Canidae except the domestic dog, bears other than the black bear, and Crocodylia. § 609.341 bars keeping one without an ODA permit, and permits had to pre-date the 2009 Act, so the practical answer for a listed animal is no. Cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of this.

wa-rcw-16-30.title: Wash. Rev. Code ch. 16.30, Dangerous Wild Animals, § 16.30.010(2) and § 16.30.030
wa-rcw-16-30.note: An enumerated definition. Felidae is limited to lions, tigers, captive-bred cougars, jaguars, cheetahs, leopards, snow leopards and clouded leopards; Canidae to wolves excluding wolf-hybrids. § 16.30.030: 'A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal', grandfathering lawful possession before 22 July 2007.

oh-935-01.title: Ohio Rev. Code § 935.01, Dangerous Wild Animals and Restricted Snakes definitions
oh-935-01.note: Two enumerated lists. Dangerous wild animals need an Ohio Department of Agriculture wildlife shelter permit; anything on neither list needs no state permit. Restricted snakes are constrictors of 12 feet or more plus venomous families.

tx-822-101.title: Tex. Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) and § 822.103, Dangerous Wild Animals
tx-822-101.note: A closed species list. § 822.103: 'a person may not own, harbor, or have custody or control of a dangerous wild animal for any purpose unless the person holds a certificate of registration for that animal issued by an animal registration agency', plus liability insurance of at least $100,000 per occurrence and caging standards.

mi-large-carnivore.title: Mich. Comp. Laws ch. 287, Large Carnivore Act and Wolf-dog Cross Act
mi-large-carnivore.note: Michigan splits this across three bodies of law: the Large Carnivore Act, the Wolf-dog Cross Act, and Part 413 of the Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act. Penalties run to misdemeanour charges, fines up to $2,000 per animal and forfeiture.

il-720-48-10.title: 720 ILCS 5/48-10, Dangerous animals
il-720-48-10.note: A closed species list plus a blanket bar on primates. Exemptions: lawful primate possession before 1 January 2011 if registered, and a single service capuchin for a permanently disabled person with severe mobility impairment. Illinois is a home rule state, so municipal ordinances matter here more than most.

mn-346-155.title: Minn. Stat. § 346.155, Possessing regulated animals
mn-346-155.note: 'Regulated animal' is all members of Felidae except the domestic cat, all bears, and all non-human primates, plus any hybrid or cross between a listed animal and a domestic animal and all subsequent generations. Possession is unlawful unless held on or before 1 January 2005 in compliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act. A knowing violation is a gross misdemeanour: up to two years imprisonment or a $5,000 fine.

nv-nac-503.title: Nev. Admin. Code § 503.110 (prohibited species) and § 503.140 (species needing no permit)
nv-nac-503.note: Two lists: 503.110 prohibits, 503.140 names species that may be possessed, transported, imported and exported without a permit. Nevada counties and cities are frequently stricter than the state, notably Clark County, Henderson and Las Vegas.

va-4vac15-30-40.title: 4 Va. Admin. Code § 15-30-40, Importation requirements, possession, and sale of nonnative (exotic) animals
va-4vac15-30-40.note: Virginia permits by table. Subsection A requires a special permit from the department for every animal listed in it, on the ground that the board has declared the species predatory or undesirable because releasing it would harm Virginia's native fish and wildlife. Subsection B grandfathers asterisked animals held before 1 July 1992 if they were declared in writing by 1 January 1993, renewable every five years and not transferable. Subsection C then carves the monk parakeet back out.

md-10-621.title: Md. Code, Criminal Law § 10-621, Importing, selling or possessing certain animals
md-10-621.note: Misdemeanour: a fine up to $1,000 for an individual, $10,000 otherwise, and the animal may be seized immediately with costs falling on the keeper unless the seizure proves unjustified. Counties and municipalities may be stricter. Note COMAR 15.11.16.01, which is titled List of Prohibited Animals, is an agriculture rule about feral swine only and is not the exotic pet provision.

nm-19-35-7.title: N.M. Admin. Code 19.35.7, Importation of Live Non-domesticated Animals, Birds and Fish
nm-19-35-7.note: Four groups. Group I is semi-domesticated and needs no importation permit; Group IV is 'dangerous, invasive, undesirable, state or federal listed threatened, endangered, a furbearer or any other species of concern' and is barred to the general public, allowed only for scientific study, restoration, zoological display, temporary events, service animals or qualified experts. The operative default: 'Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.' The group assignments themselves live in a separate Director's Species Importation List, roughly 27 pages, which I could not obtain.

vt-reg-881.title: Vermont Regulation 881 (12-021 Code Vt. R.), Governing the Importation and Possession of Wild Animals, with 10 V.S.A. § 4709
vt-reg-881.note: Closed list. § 4709 bars bringing in, transporting or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorisation. Reg 881: 'the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity, except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes' unless the species is designated domestic, a domestic pet, or unrestricted. The Unrestricted Wild Animals List is maintained separately on the department website and was not obtainable.

vt-20-3541.title: Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 20, § 3541(3), definition of ferret
vt-20-3541.note: Ferrets were legalised in 1989 and are defined as a domestic pet alongside dogs and cats, limited to 'the European ferret Mustela putorious furo'.

ut-r657-3.title: Utah Admin. Code R657-3 / R657-3b, Collection, Importation, Transportation and Possession of Animals
ut-r657-3.note: Three tiers: noncontrolled needs no certificate of registration, controlled and prohibited both do. Species assignments are in Table 3b-1 on the division's Certificates of Registration page. A reclassification from noncontrolled to controlled or prohibited allows a COR for continued possession of an animal already held.

de-3900.title: 7 Del. Admin. Code 3900, Wildlife, exotic animal provisions
de-3900.note: An exotic animal is 'ecologically foreign to Delaware, but allowed for possession, sale, and exhibition if a permit has been issued by the Department', covering live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals, and live reptiles not native to the state. A prohibited sublist sits on top, barred to everyone outside parks, zoos, aquariums, museums and research facilities. Administered by the State Veterinarian.

tn-70-4-403.title: Tenn. Code Ann. § 70-4-403, Classifications of wildlife
tn-70-4-403.note: Three classes. Class I is 'all species inherently dangerous to humans such as wolves, bears, lions and poisonous snakes', possessable only by zoos, circuses and commercial propagators. Class II is 'native species, except those listed in other classes'. Class III is everything else and needs no wildlife permit, only whatever the Department of Agriculture requires. The catch-all sitting at Class III rather than Class II is what makes Tennessee permissive.

ar-unrestricted.title: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
ar-unrestricted.note: Species that may be held in captivity without a permit, named individually with binomials. One of the cleanest primary sources of any state for this purpose.

id-020427.title: IDAPA 02.04.27, Idaho Department of Agriculture, Rules Governing Deleterious Exotic Animals
id-020427.note: Section 100.01 bars possession of a deleterious exotic animal without a possession permit from the Administrator. Sections 401 to 412 are the list itself, by taxon.

id-130110.title: IDAPA 13.01.10, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Rules Governing Importation, Possession, Release, Sale, or Salvage of Wildlife
id-130110.note: Section 010.06 defines conventional pets, which sit outside the wildlife permit regime. Unusually explicit: it names ferrets, hedgehogs and sugar gliders in the rule text.

ia-717F.title: Iowa Code Chapter 717F, Dangerous Wild Animals
ia-717F.note: § 717F.3 bars owning, possessing, breeding or importing a dangerous wild animal. § 717F.1(5) defines the class by family and order rather than by species name, so the boundaries are read off the taxonomy. § 717F.4 grandfathers animals already owned on 1 July 2007.

ia-481A.title: Iowa Code Chapter 481A, Wildlife Conservation
ia-481A.note: The native wildlife side. § 481A.67 governs taking turtles.

ky-301-2-082.title: 301 KAR 2:082, Transportation and holding of live exotic wildlife
ky-301-2-082.note: Three lists. Section 4(1) is prohibited species, injurious to native ecosystems. Section 4(2) is inherently dangerous exotic wildlife. Section 7 is the permit-exempt list. Anything on none of the three may be possessed, but a transportation permit is needed to bring it into the state. KRS 65.877, cited in the regulation itself, lets local governments prohibit inherently dangerous wildlife outright.

ri-250-40-05-3.title: 250-RICR-40-05-3, Rules and Regulations Governing the Importation and Possession of Wild Animals
ri-250-40-05-3.note: One of the most species-specific schemes in the country. § 3.6 defines domestic animals, § 3.7 sets general prohibitions, § 3.9 governs permits, and § 3.17 is the long exempt list of animals that need no exotic animal possession permit. Anything not domestic, not native and not on the § 3.17 list needs a permit.

nh-fis800.title: New Hampshire Code of Administrative Rules, Fis 800, Importation and Possession of Wildlife
nh-fis800.note: Fis 804.02 is the non-controlled possession list, needing no permit. Fis 804.05 is the controlled table, and the number beside each species is the permittee category allowed to hold it. Category 1 is an individual, category 5 is an exhibitor, so a species marked 5 alone cannot be kept by a private person at all.

mo-578-023.title: Missouri Revised Statutes § 578.023, Keeping a dangerous wild animal
mo-578-023.note: Missouri does not ban these animals. It requires that they be registered with the local law enforcement agency in the county where they are kept. Failure to register is the offence.

mo-3csr10-9.title: 3 CSR 10-9, Missouri Wildlife Code: Confined Wildlife
mo-3csr10-9.note: Class I is native Missouri mammals, reptiles and amphibians plus birds native to the continental United States. Class II is the venomous natives, mountain lion, wolf and black bear. Class III is cervids. An animal that is none of these is outside the Wildlife Code entirely.

ks-32-1301.title: K.S.A. 32-1301, Dangerous regulated animals; definitions
ks-32-1301.note: Kansas restricts three things and nothing else. The definition is short enough to read in full, which is what makes it useful: everything outside it is untouched by the Act.

sc-47-2.title: S.C. Code Title 47, Chapter 2, Large Wild Cats, Non-Native Bears and Great Apes
sc-47-2.note: The 2018 Act. It is narrow on purpose: genus Panthera, non-native bears, great apes, and hybrids of those. Anyone in lawful possession before 1 January 2018 could register with the local animal control authority and keep the animal for its life.

sc-50-16.title: S.C. Code Title 50, Chapter 16, Importation and Possession of Wildlife
sc-50-16.note: § 50-16-20 requires a permit to bring in certain groups of live wildlife, chiefly furbearers, cervids, pigs, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. § 50-16-60 then exempts a named list of pet trade animals from even that.

mt-87-5-7.title: Montana Code Annotated Title 87, Chapter 5, Part 7, Importation, Introduction, and Transplantation of Wildlife
mt-87-5-7.note: Montana runs a white list, which is unusual. § 87-5-705(1) says a person may not import, possess or sell any exotic wildlife unless it is allowed by law or commission rule, so an animal that appears on none of the three lists is not permitted rather than unregulated. § 87-5-706 is the statutory noncontrolled list and § 87-5-702 puts rodents, cats, dogs and Eurasian ferrets outside the scheme as domestic animals.

mt-arm-12-6-22.title: Administrative Rules of Montana, Subchapter 12.6.22, Exotic Wildlife
mt-arm-12-6-22.note: 12.6.2205 is the noncontrolled list, 12.6.2208 the controlled list, 12.6.2215 the prohibited list. The noncontrolled definition at 12.6.2201(8) expressly preserves county and city ordinances.

wv-19-34.title: W. Va. Code § 19-34, Dangerous Wild Animals Act
wv-19-34.note: Unusual structure, and the reason most entries here are unclear. § 19-34-4 bans possession of a dangerous wild animal, but § 19-34-2 defines the term by character rather than by species and § 19-34-5 directs a three member board to create the actual list by legislative rule. The statute itself names no animal. Until that list is confirmed in force, the ban has no species attached to it.

ak-5aac92-029.title: 5 AAC 92.029, Permit for possessing live game
ak-5aac92-029.note: The strictest structure in the country and the clearest. Subsection (a) bars possessing live game without a permit, (b) is a short clean list of species needing no permit, and (c) then removes the escape hatch: the department may not issue a permit for any game animal for use as a pet. So an animal missing from the clean list cannot be kept, permit or not.

sd-12-68-18.title: ARSD 12:68:18, Nondomestic Animal Control
sd-12-68-18.note: Two separate requirements sit in the same chapter and are easy to conflate. An entry permit, free and obtainable by telephone, is required to import any nondomestic animal. A possession permit, ten dollars per animal, is required only for the mammal families listed in 12:68:18:03. The only outright prohibition is the raccoon dog.

al-220-2-26.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26, Restrictions On Possession, Sale, Importation And/Or Release Of Certain Animals And Fish
al-220-2-26.note: A prohibited list rather than a permitted one, last amended October 2024. Two clauses do most of the work for pet keepers: everything the federal government lists as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act is banned by reference, and a group of species is banned specifically when it comes from outside Alabama.

in-312-9-11.title: 312 IAC 9-11, Wild Animal Possession Permits
in-312-9-11.note: Three classes by risk. Class I is rabbits and squirrels, Class II is a long and specific list of small wild cats plus Indiana's furbearers, Class III is wolves, bears, all other wild cats, venomous reptiles and large crocodilians. Both the Class II and Class III lists end with the same sentence exempting hybrids with a domestic dog or cat, which is the clearest hybrid answer any state gives.

nd-36-01.title: North Dakota Century Code Chapter 36-01, Board of Animal Health
nd-36-01.note: The chapter names only three restrictions relevant to pets: skunks and raccoons may not be kept at all, mountain lions and wolves need a tattooed identification number, and the board is to make rules on primates. § 36-01-08.1 says the board may require a licence for nontraditional livestock, meaning any wildlife held in confinement, but the wording is permissive.

nd-48-1.title: North Dakota Administrative Code Title 48.1, State Board of Animal Health
nd-48-1.note: The old title 48, which carried the nontraditional livestock category system, is repealed. What replaced it is a set of importation health chapters. Chapter 48.1-13-02 covers everything else and asks only for a certificate of veterinary inspection and an importation permit number from the state veterinarian.

wy-ch10.title: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 10, Importation and Possession of Live Warm-Blooded Wildlife
wy-ch10.note: Two closed lists do the work. Domestic animals and domesticated animals are both defined by enumeration, with the phrase for the purpose of this regulation, only the following animals are considered domestic. Anything on neither list is wildlife, and Section 13(d) leaves it to a permit that may be authorised upon approval.

wy-ch69.title: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 69, Importation and Possession of Live Cold-Blooded Wildlife
wy-ch69.note: Section 10(a)(i) is the sentence that matters for reptile keepers: amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 need no permit at all.

ms-40-2-8-3.title: 40 Miss. Admin. Code Part 2, Rule 8.3, Regulations For Animals Inherently Dangerous To Humans
ms-40-2-8-3.note: A short list drawn by genus and family, covering apes and some monkeys, wolves and three wild dogs, bears, the wolverine, hyenas, the big cats, elephants, rhinos, hippos and African buffalo. Nothing smaller appears. The rule also notes that since the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act took effect in December 2022 no new big cat permits are issued at all.

la-76-v-115.title: LAC 76:V.115, Possession of Potentially Dangerous Wild Quadrupeds, Big Exotic Cats, and Non-Human Primates
la-76-v-115.note: A short mammal ban: three bears, two wolves, wolf dog hybrids, all non-human primates, and six big cats with their subspecies and hybrids. Existing permit holders were grandfathered but may not acquire more.

la-76-xv-101.title: LAC 76:XV.101, Reptiles and Amphibians, Recreational and Commercial Harvests; Prohibitions
la-76-xv-101.note: Rewritten in January 2025 and now one of the strictest reptile rules in the country. Three tiers: prohibited nonnative species, restricted nonnative species needing a permit, and a general rule that any constrictor over eight feet needs a restricted snake permit.

ok-800-25-25-3.title: OAC 800:25-25-3, Exemptions
ok-800-25-25-3.note: Navigate to Title 800, Chapter 25, Subchapter 25, Section 800:25-25-3. One of the most permissive exemption lists in the country, and one of the very few that names the fennec fox individually. Note what the exemptions are from: permits and breeder licences, not a ban. An unexempt animal is licensable, not prohibited.

ne-166-nac-8.title: 166 NAC 8, Nebraska Game and Parks Commission, Keeping Wildlife in Captivity
ne-166-nac-8.note: Browse to Game and Parks Commission, Title 166 Wildlife Regulations, Chapter 8. Two lists that must not be conflated. § 001.01B lists the native wild birds and mammals that may be held under a Captive Wildlife Permit. § 001.08A is a separate closed list of wildlife that may be imported into the state, and a non-native animal missing from it cannot lawfully be brought in.

hi-conditional.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules, List of Conditionally Approved Animals (Hawaii Department of Agriculture official PDF)
hi-conditional.note: The list that matters most for pet keepers and the one almost never quoted. Conditional approval means importation and possession are allowed subject to the conditions the Board of Agriculture sets, unlike the restricted list, which is research and exhibition only.

nc-153a-131.title: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 153A-131, Possession or harboring of dangerous animals
nc-153a-131.note: The reason North Carolina looks unregulated from the state house and is anything but on the ground. A county may by ordinance regulate, restrict or prohibit possession of animals dangerous to persons or property, and many have. Your county code is the operative law here, not the General Statutes.

nc-14-417.title: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-417, Regulation of ownership or use of venomous reptiles
nc-14-417.note: North Carolina's entire statewide exotic animal statute, and it reaches venomous reptiles only. It does not ban them either: it requires an escape-proof, bite-proof, lockable enclosure, a label reading Venomous Reptile Inside naming the species and the right antivenin, a written bite protocol kept in sight, and immediate notice to law enforcement on an escape. Nothing else in the General Statutes restricts keeping an exotic animal.

pa-2961.title: 34 Pa.C.S. § 2961, Game and Wildlife Code, exotic wildlife definition
pa-2961.note: The definition names bears, coyotes, lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars, wolves and their crossbreeds, and none of the animals in this dataset. The entire prohibition rests on four words earlier in the sentence, includes, but is not limited to, which the Game Commission reads as reaching small exotic mammals. That is an agency interpretation of a definition rather than anything a legislature wrote about these species, which is why bills to reverse it keep being introduced.

hi-hrs150A-6-2.title: Hawaii Revised Statutes § 150A-6.2, Animal import
hi-hrs150A-6-2.note: The statute behind the lists. Subsection (c) is the default rule: anything not on the conditionally approved, restricted or prohibited list is prohibited until the board reviews it.

mt-87-5-116.title: Montana Code Annotated § 87-5-116, Limited taking of certain nongame wildlife for commercial purposes
mt-87-5-116.note: Restricts commercial taking of native Montana amphibians and reptiles. It does not reach personal possession, which is why native species sit outside the exotic wildlife permit regime.

ak-as16-05-940.title: Alaska Statutes § 16.05.940(19), definition of game
ak-as16-05-940.note: Game means any species of bird, reptile and mammal. Amphibians and invertebrates are outside the definition, so the live game permit rule at 5 AAC 92.029 does not reach them at all.

wa-wac-220-640-200.title: WAC 220-640-200, Deleterious exotic wildlife
wa-wac-220-640-200.note: Washington's second exotic animal rule. Checked and found to cover only ungulates, mongooses, wild boar, peccary and the mute swan, so it does not reach any common exotic pet.

VA.quote: Exception for certain monk parakeets. No permit is required for monk parakeets (quakers) that have been captive bred and are closed-banded with a seamless band.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit,

SC.quote: 6. shell parakeets 7. love birds 8. cockatiels 9. parrots

IN.note: No bird appears on any of the three class lists.

WY.quote: a permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the following live warm-blooded wildlife in Wyoming... (iii) Monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus);

MS.note: No bird appears on the list.

OK.quote: The following list of birds shall be exempt from import and export requirements... (2) Psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets and budgerigars).
OK.note: Cleared by group with no monk parakeet exception.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage. For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird.
NE.note: A neat piece of drafting to watch for. The importation list ends with All Cage and Aviary Birds, and the definitions section removes the monk parakeet from that category by name, so the one bird excluded from the definition is the one bird that cannot be imported.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Your county code is the operative layer.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No bird appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal permit list here.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: A monk parakeet is a common cage bird and captive bred, so it clears the bird category. DC is one of the few places that does not single the species out.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The bird list runs to dozens of parrots by name and the monk parakeet is not among them, so it stays inside Code 09.02 rather than being exempted. This is the usual pattern: the monk parakeet is the one parrot states single out, because established colonies damage electrical infrastructure.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No bird of any kind is on the dangerous wild animal list, and Ohio has no separate monk parakeet provision, so the species is unrestricted here while most states single it out.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: No bird is a potentially dangerous wild animal, and the only bird on the deleterious exotic wildlife rule is the mute swan. Washington is one of the states where the monk parakeet is simply unregulated.

CA.quote: Domestic cats and hybrids of domestic cats are not restricted

DC.quote: Domestic cats, excluding hybrids with ocelots or margays
DC.note: The Bengal derives from the Asian leopard cat, which is neither.

NYC.quote: All cats other than domesticated cats (Felis catus), including ... any hybrid offspring of a wild cat and domesticated cat.

NY.note: Felidae hybrids are wild animals except registered hybrids with no wild felid ancestry for five or more generations, so an F5 or later Bengal qualifies. NYC bans all wild-cat hybrids regardless.

MN.note: The definition expressly reaches 'any hybrid or cross between an animal listed as prohibited and a domestic animal and offspring from all subsequent generations', so unlike New York there is no generation at which a Bengal falls out.

MD.quote: hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds
MD.note: Maryland draws the line by weight rather than by generation. A Bengal under 30 lb is outside the prohibition, which most Bengals are.

ID.quote: Geoffroy's Cat (Felis geoffroyi). Margay (Felis wiedii). Ocelot (Felis pardalis). Serval (Felis serval).
ID.note: The small felidae list is these four. The Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal, Prionailurus bengalensis, is not on it, and cats are conventional pets under IDAPA 13.01.10.

IA.quote: The bengal must be the fourth or later filial generation of offspring with the first filial generation being the offspring of a domestic cat and an Asian leopard cat, and each subsequent generation being the offspring of a domestic cat.
IA.note: F4 and later are carved out of the definition. F1 to F3 are dangerous wild animals and are banned.

KY.quote: Lions, jaguars, leopards, or tigers (Genus Panthera); Lynx (Genus Lynx);
KY.note: Prionailurus bengalensis appears on neither list, and the hybrid clause in Section 4(2)(v) reaches only hybrids of species in that subsection.

RI.quote: Domestic Cat (Felis catus) excluding hybrids with wild felines,
RI.note: An F1 cross is plainly excluded from the domestic animal list and then caught by the § 3.9(B) bar on permits for Carnivora hybrids. A late generation Bengal is the offspring of two domestic cats, so on the § 3.6(A)(13) definition of hybrid it arguably is not one. The regulation sets no filial generation cut off the way Iowa and New York do. Ask the Division of Agriculture before buying.

NH.quote: 5   Tiger; Golden Tabby, Siberian, White Siberian, Bengal   Panthera tigeris

MO.quote: any lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, Canada lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi
MO.note: The statute names species and says nothing about hybrids or filial generations.

KS.quote: Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof;
KS.note: The hybrid clause attaches to those six species. Leopard here means Panthera pardus, not the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal.

SC.quote: Family Felidae, Genus panthera—all lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cougars, cheetahs, snow leopards, and clouded leopards;

WV.quote: "Domestic animal" means an animal which, through extremely long association with humans, has been bred to a degree which has resulted in genetic changes affecting the temperament, color, conformation or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes it unique and distinguishable from a wild individual of its species, and includes an animal that has been bred as a companion animal.

KY.note: Kentucky regulates snakes by venom, not by size, so the giant constrictors are untouched by this regulation.

RI.quote: except the Emerald Tree Boa (Corallus caninus), Green Tree Python (Chondropython spp.), African Rock Python (Python sebae), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus) and all species of Anaconda (Eunectes spp.).
RI.note: The exception list names the reticulated and African rock pythons but not Python bivittatus, so the Burmese python stays permit free.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: New Hampshire draws its reptile line at crocodilians and venom, not at size.

MO.quote: any deadly, dangerous, or poisonous reptile, or any deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet long, in any place other than a properly maintained zoological park, circus, scientific, or educational institution, research laboratory, veterinary hospital, or animal refuge, unless he or she has registered such animals with the local law enforcement agency in the county in which the animal is kept
MO.note: Not banned, but an adult Burmese python comfortably passes eight feet, at which point it must be registered with the county law enforcement agency. There is no state permit and no fee, just the registration.

KS.quote: all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: Kansas sets no length limit on constrictors, unlike Missouri next door.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles
SC.note: Written as a single word covering the whole class, with no carve out for giant constrictors.

MT.quote: Indian python (including the Burmese python) – Python molurus;
MT.note: Named in the parenthesis, so there is no argument about the split of Python molurus and Python bivittatus. The reticulated python, African rock python, amethystine python and green anaconda are prohibited alongside it.

WV.quote: (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes;
WV.note: An adult Burmese python is well over six feet, so it falls inside the category the board was told to consider.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The clearance is written to include crocodiles and alligators by name, so size is plainly not the test. Venom is.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama does not name the species itself. It adopts the federal injurious wildlife list, which has included Python bivittatus since 2012, so the federal listing does the work.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.
IN.note: Indiana applies a length test to crocodilians and none at all to constrictors.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules, and North Dakota sets no constrictor length limit.

WY.quote: An importation/possession permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the live cold-blooded wildlife in this section... (a) Injurious wildlife listed in 50 CFR § 16.
WY.note: Adopted from the federal injurious list, which has covered Python bivittatus since 2012. The reticulated python and the green anaconda arrive by the same route.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian, so Mississippi sets no constrictor size limit in this rule.

LA.quote: vii. Burmese Python (Python bivittatus);

grandfathered.detail: Registration within 365 days of the rule taking effect, no breeding, no further acquisition.

OK.quote: except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations
OK.note: The exemption turns on the federal injurious wildlife listing, which covers Python bivittatus. Losing the exemption means permits and a breeder's licence apply, not that the animal is banned.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Non-venomous, so it clears on the wording. The traditionally kept in the home qualifier is the only obvious argument against, and DC sets no size limit.

HI.quote: Serpentes (all species in suborder, except for two male nonvenomous snakes for exhibition in a government zoo, and for four sterile male brown tree snakes, Boiga irregularis, for research or training of snake detector dogs by the department)
HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder, with two narrow carve outs that are both institutional. HRS § 150A-6(3) repeats the bar at statute level. No snake of any species or size is keepable here.

ME.note: The snake section lists pythons individually and neither Python bivittatus nor Python molurus is among them. The asterisk footnote would exclude it in any case, since the Burmese python has been federal injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act since 2012.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Ball Python (Python regius) ... Blood Python (Python curtus) ... Bornean Shorttail and Red Blood Pythons (Python breitensteini, P. brongersmai)
AR.note: Arkansas clears pythons species by species and by genus for the Australasian group. Python bivittatus is on none of those entries, so the Burmese python stays restricted. It is federal injurious wildlife as well, which bars bringing one across a state line.

CA.quote: Class Reptilia   Reptiles: (A) Order Crocodilia ... (C) Family Elapidae ... (D) Family Viperidae ... (E) Family Crotalidae-Pitvipers: All nonnative species (D) ... (F) Family Colubridae
CA.note: California restricts snakes by family and only the venomous ones, plus three colubrid genera. Pythonidae is not listed, so the Burmese python is unrestricted under state law. Federal law is the real constraint: it has been injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act since 2012, so it cannot be brought across a state line.

WA.quote: Family atractaspidae, all species; Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus; Family elapidae, all species ... Family hydrophiidae, all species ... Family viperidae, all species
WA.note: Every snake family Washington restricts is venomous. Pythonidae and Boidae are absent entirely, so there is no state limit on a large constrictor, by species or by length. The federal injurious wildlife listing still bars bringing a Burmese python across a state line.

MA.note: Named on the exemption list by binomial. The criteria for getting on it include posing no significant ecological risk if released and needing no more care than a common domestic animal.

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a rodent. Worth knowing because Colorado does require a permit for a degu, so the two states differ.

ID.quote: South American Rodents. All South American rodents except guinea pigs and chinchillas.
ID.note: Octodon degus is a Chilean rodent and is not one of the two exceptions, so it is a deleterious exotic animal needing a possession permit.

KY.note: On neither restricted list. Kentucky bans prairie dogs and the Gambian pouched rat by name, so the rodent list is specific rather than general.

RI.quote: Degu (Octodon degus),

NH.quote: Degaus (Octodon degus);
NH.note: Spelled Degaus in the rule as filed.

MO.note: Not Missouri wildlife and not on the dangerous wild animal list.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal.

SC.note: Outside every group named in the import permit provision.

MT.quote: Degu (bush-tailed rat) - Octodon degus;

WV.quote: that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal... for use as a pet
AK.note: The clean list clears the guinea pig, the cavy, the chinchilla and two gerbils. The degu is not among them.

SD.quote: A permit from the board is required to import nondomestic animals.
SD.note: No rodent appears on the possession permit list.

AL.quote: Any of the following from any area outside the state of Alabama; ...species of skunk, wild rodent, or strain of wild turkey
AL.note: Wild rodent is not defined anywhere in the rule. A pet degu is captive bred, but Octodon degus is a wild species with no domesticated lineage behind it, unlike the hamster or the guinea pig. Ask the Division of Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries before buying.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.

WY.quote: A permit may be authorized upon approval for other warm-blooded wildlife unless otherwise specified in this regulation.
WY.note: The domesticated list clears the chinchilla, the guinea pig, the gerbil, the hamster, the mouse and the rat, but not the degu.

MS.note: No rodent appears on the list.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: The following wildlife species are exempt from import and export permits, commercial wildlife breeders licenses, noncommercial wildlife breeders licenses and commercial hunting area license requirements
OK.note: The list clears chinchillas, gerbils, guinea pigs, hamsters, mice and rats but not the degu, so it stays inside the permit and breeder licence regime rather than being banned.

NE.note: Named on the importation list, which few states do.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, so no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

DC.quote: Domesticated rodents and rabbits
DC.note: The rodent category is limited to domesticated ones. A degu is a wild species bred in captivity rather than a domesticated one, which puts it in the same position as the capybara and outside the category.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: Octodon is on no Hawaii list. The contrast with the chinchilla and the guinea pig, both conditionally approved, is a good illustration that Hawaii's lists work species by species rather than by how domesticated an animal looks.

ME.note: Named individually, which is worth noting because the degu is barred outright in California and Georgia and is a legal grey area in several other states.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: Octodon degus is absent while the chinchilla, guinea pig and hamsters are all named, so the omission looks deliberate rather than accidental.

CA.quote: Order Rodentia-Hamsters, Field Mice, Voles, Muskrats, Gerbils, Squirrels, Chipmunks, Woodchucks, and Prairie Dogs. All species (D), except: ... b. Domesticated races of golden hamsters ... and dwarf hamsters of the Genus Phodopus ... d. Domesticated races of guinea pigs of the species Cavia porcellus ... e. Domesticated races of chinchillas of the species Chinchilla laniger
CA.note: California restricts the whole order and then names five exceptions. Octodon degus is not one of them, which is why the degu is barred here while the chinchilla, a close relative and also a South American caviomorph, is expressly cleared. Section 671.1 permits exist but are not issued for pet keeping.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Ohio does not maintain an approved species list, so a rodent that is not a dangerous wild animal needs no clearance. This is the opposite of California, where the degu is barred by falling inside a restricted order.

WA.quote: (a) Class mammalia (i) Order carnivora ... (iii) Order primates ... (iv) Order proboscidae
WA.note: Washington keeps no approved species list, so a rodent that is not a potentially dangerous wild animal needs no clearance.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess, display, offer for sale, trade, barter, exchange, or adoption, or give as a household pet, any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: The seven permitted categories are dogs, cats, domesticated rodents and rabbits, captive-bred common cage birds, non-venomous snakes, fish and turtles, ferrets and racing pigeons. No amphibian fits any of them, so the axolotl is barred by omission.

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Ambystomidae
HI.note: Named individually on the conditionally approved list, so importation and possession are allowed subject to Department of Agriculture conditions. A rare yes from a state that bans most exotics by default.

RI.quote: All persons other than a bona fide researcher, or a licensed pet shop and their transportation agents are prohibited from possessing any species of exotic amphibians unless they are kept indoors as pets in a manner that will prevent their escape or liberation into the wild.
RI.note: Treated as an exotic amphibian: indoors only, and importation limited to pet shops and researchers.

NH.quote: Amphibians, exotic;
NH.note: Exotic amphibians are non-controlled for possession. The controlled table covers New Hampshire's own Ambystoma species, and the axolotl is Mexican.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of salamanders not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: (i) Ambystomatidae (mole salamanders);
MT.note: Cleared by family on the statutory noncontrolled list, which matters in Montana because anything not classified cannot be imported at all.

CA.quote: Genus Ambystoma (nonnative tiger salamander group)-(D)
CA.note: Ambystoma mexicanum sits in the listed genus. The parenthetical describes the group the restriction was aimed at rather than narrowing it, and none of the permit types in § 671.1 covers pet keeping, so there is no route.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian, so no amphibian is reached by it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: Amphibians are exempted as a class from the import permit in the same sentence as reptiles.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No amphibian appears anywhere in the chapter. The prohibitions are skunks and raccoons.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No amphibian is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. No amphibian is reached by it, and § 153A-131 leaves the rest to counties.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list. The only amphibians named are the cane toad and the African clawed frog, both as injurious species.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No amphibian appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition covers canids, hyenas, felids, bears, rhinos, elephants, primates, crocodilians, some squamates and swine. No amphibian appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only. A free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

VA.quote: Ambystomatidae   All species, except Ambystoma mexicanum   All mole salamanders, except Mexican axolotl
VA.note: One of the few places in the country where the axolotl is written into a rule as an exception rather than a target. Virginia restricts every other mole salamander and carves this one out by binomial and by common name.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: The prohibited amphibians are the Cuban treefrog, the cane toad and the African clawed frog. The axolotl is not among them.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... native to the continental United States, and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: Mexican, so not native to Missouri and outside Class I. Missouri's own Ambystoma species are a different question.

WY.quote: An importation/possession permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the live cold-blooded wildlife in this section... (a) Injurious wildlife listed in 50 CFR § 16.
WY.note: Ambystoma mexicanum is inside the same federal genus listing, so Wyoming will not issue a permit. Section 8 is absolute: it does not offer a permit route, it forecloses one.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A non-venomous amphibian that is not Idaho native wildlife, so it is a conventional pet and § 200.06 exempts it from any Department permit. Idaho's approach is unusually readable: one definition does the work that other states spread over three lists.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: Outside the definition of game, so outside the clean list. This is the reverse of the usual pattern, where Alaska is the hardest state to satisfy.

ME.quote: Amphibia (Amphibians)   Captive Bred Origin Only ... Anura (Frogs And Toads)
ME.note: Same gap as the tiger salamander: the amphibian list is frogs and toads only. The axolotl is also IUCN Critically Endangered, which the footnote would catch even if a salamander order existed.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife...
AR.note: No amphibian section exists on the unrestricted list, so a non-native salamander is neither exempted nor addressed. Note separately that federal law at 50 CFR 16.14 bars bringing any Ambystoma across a state line.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Outside Chapter 935 and not native to Ohio. The federal injurious wildlife listing of the genus Ambystoma is the constraint that matters, and it bites on importing or shipping one rather than on keeping it.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Amphibians are outside the statute. As with every state, the live constraint on the axolotl is federal: 50 CFR 16.14 lists the whole genus as injurious wildlife.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Turtles are one of the seven permitted categories, and the clause turns on keeping the animal for pleasure rather than commercially.

HI.quote: Terrapene (all species in genus except T. coahuila)
HI.note: The whole genus is conditionally approved apart from the Coahuilan box turtle, which sits on the restricted Part B list instead.

RI.quote: The possession of native turtles is restricted to those institutions identified within § 3.7(C) of this Part... Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina),
RI.note: Native to Rhode Island, so possession is limited to the Department, USFWS, AZA zoos, research institutions and USDA licensed exhibitors. Not a pet species here.

LA.quote: Box Turtles—Terrapene sp.
LA.note: A restricted turtle. No more than ten restricted turtles in total and no more than two of any one species, and § 101.G.2.a.ii separately caps native box turtles at two regardless of species. A basic recreational fishing licence is needed to collect one.

NH.quote: 5   Eastern box turtle   Terrapene carolina carolina
NH.note: Permittee category 5 is an exhibitor, with no category 1 for an individual, so a private keeper cannot be permitted for one.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian. Mississippi restricts no reptile under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit, and its only other exotic pet statute reaches genus Panthera, non-native bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: That sentence, plus tattooing for mountain lions and wolves and rulemaking for primates, is the whole of North Dakota's prohibition list. No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes. Constrictors, lizards and turtles are untouched at any size.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently dangerous list. The only reptiles on either are gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing here falls in those categories.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States, and those species of mammals (except bison and those listed in 3 CSR 10-9.240 and 3 CSR 10-9.250) and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: Both the three-toed and the ornate box turtle are native to Missouri, which puts them in Class I. Permits issue only for species on the Approved Confined Wildlife Species List.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: The ornate box turtle reaches southeastern Wyoming, so the same split applies: no permit for captive-bred stock kept privately, while the nongame regulation governs collecting one.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ... (v) Emydidae (pond turtles)
MT.note: Box turtles are Emydidae, so the family is cleared, but every category on this list is gated on being tropical and subtropical, and both the eastern and the ornate box turtle are temperate North American animals. The qualifier looks deliberate, since a temperate species could survive a Montana release in a way a tropical one could not. Ask Fish, Wildlife and Parks before buying.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: No Terrapene is native to Idaho, so the captured from the wild in Idaho carve-out does not bite, and a box turtle is a conventional pet needing no permit.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list is almost entirely species by species, then clears the whole of Class Reptilia in one line so long as the animal is not venomous. A box turtle needs no permit.

ME.note: No Terrapene appears anywhere on the list. The only match for the words box turtle is the Amboina box turtle, which is a Cuora and a different animal. The eastern box turtle is also a species of special concern in Maine, so its own native status is part of the picture.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife in compliance with Code Chapters 26.00, 27.00, 29.00, 30.00, 31.00, 32.00, 33.00, 34.00, 35.00...
AR.note: Both the three-toed and the ornate box turtle are native to Arkansas, and a terrestrial native turtle is neither on the unrestricted list nor inside the aquatic wildlife carve-out. Arkansas's native wildlife rules govern, and this document does not reach them.

CA.quote: Family Chelyridae-Snapping Turtles: All species (D)
CA.note: Snapping turtles are the only restricted family in Testudines, so a box turtle is unrestricted. The spelling Chelyridae in the regulation is a long-standing typo for Chelydridae.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Chapter 935 does not reach it. The eastern box turtle is native to Ohio and taking one from the wild is governed by the Division of Wildlife rather than by the exotic animal law.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: No Terrapene is native to Washington and none is listed, so nothing in RCW 16.30 applies.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Permitted as a turtle. The federal four-inch sale rule still applies to buying a hatchling anywhere in the country.

HI.cite: List of Restricted Animals, Part B
HI.note: Part B is the restricted list for private and commercial use, so unlike a Part A animal this one has a route, but it needs a permit rather than being freely importable.

RI.quote: All persons other than a bona fide researcher, or a licensed pet shops and their transportation agents are prohibited from possessing Red Eared Slider turtles unless they are kept indoors as pets in a manner that will prevent their escape or liberation into the wild. Keeping of these animals in any type of outdoor enclosure is prohibited.
RI.note: Keepable indoors only, and only a pet shop or a researcher may import one. Pet shops must tell buyers about the indoor requirement at the point of sale.

LA.quote: Red-eared Slider—Trachemys scripta elegans;
